articles.author: Nurbek Bekmurzaev
articles.title: In Kosovo, a new app makes reporting problems to the government fast and easy
articles.excerpt: It will cut the bureacratic red tape that plagues state institutions
articles.content:
This story by Nurbek Bekmurzaev originally appeared on Global Voices. Text licensed under CC BY 3.0. Reformatted for reading; third-party media omitted.

It will cut the bureacratic red tape that plagues state institutions

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement. 

One of the biggest barriers for people’s effective engagement with the authorities in Kosovo is a confusing and unresponsive bureaucracy. Whenever citizens want to report a problem in their community, such as potholes or illegal waste disposal, they are met with a system that requires them to know the roles and responsibilities of various state institutions and handle necessary paperwork themselves.

When submitted to the wrong agency or without proper documents, citizens’ complaints are either ignored or can take long periods to be processed, which discourages engagement and has an adverse effect on people’s trust in the government.  Ultimately, it deteriorates the already challenging situation regarding transparency, communication, and accountability of state bodies in Kosovo.

In 2026, a local non-governmental organization (NGO), Sbunker, responded to this challenge by creating an online platform called Kosovo.report to help citizens report their complaints to the authorities in a quick and easy manner. Global Voices conducted an email interview with Hana Deva, project manager at SBunker, to learn more about their initiative. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Hana Deva (HD): Sbunker is a non-governmental organization founded in 2016, focused on providing analysis and informed perspectives on important political, economic, social, and cultural issues in Kosovo and the Western Balkans.

Through our Disinfo program, we monitor local and regional media content to identify and address disinformation. Sbunker produces podcasts and other media content exploring political and social developments, philosophical, cultural, and theoretical discussions.

We joined the Digital Sparks project because we wanted to create a direct form of civic engagement through technology. This led to the development of Kosovo.report, a platform designed to give citizens a simple way to report problems and submit requests concerning their neighborhoods and local communities.

The platform is intended to act as a link between citizens and public institutions by helping these reports reach the relevant institutions and making the process more accessible to the citizens.

GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project? 

HD: Through our work in media and civic engagement, we became interested in how citizens communicate everyday problems in their communities to public institutions.

Research on public administration in Kosovo points to fragmented public service delivery, inconsistencies in administrative procedures and digital services, and continuing challenges in communication between citizens and institutions.

This can make the process of reporting an issue to the right department unclear.

Kosovo.report was developed with this challenge in mind. The idea is to give citizens a more straightforward way to report an issue, without requiring them to first determine which institution or department is responsible.

Based on the type and location of the problem, the platform is designed to route the report to the appropriate department and allow the citizen to follow what happens afterwards.

GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project? 

HD: Our main work has been the development of Kosovo.report, from the initial concept to a functional platform now being prepared for its pilot phase.

Alongside this development, we have coordinated with the Municipality of Prishtina to determine how reports should reach the appropriate departments, and prepared a Memorandum of Understanding to formalise this cooperation.

Beyond the platform, Sbunker has served as a capacity hub for other Digital Sparks project grantees during the project period. We organized meetings and an advocacy workshop where grantees worked on developing a joint advocacy event.

We also hosted a young fellow, Bora Dibra, from the Albanian organization IRSH (Young Intellectuals, Hope), for a one-month fellowship focused on digital civic engagement, media literacy, and participatory advocacy.

GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

HD: The project has allowed Sbunker to expand the way we approach civic engagement. Much of our work traditionally focused on informing citizens and creating public debate through publications.

Through Kosovo.report, we are developing a tool that takes this a step further by giving citizens a channel through which they can raise problems in their communities and have their reports directed to the relevant departments.

The next step will be the pilot of Kosovo.report in the capital, Prishtina, where we will be able to test the platform with citizens, gather their feedback, and identify what needs to be improved.

GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

HD: Developing Kosovo.report has given us experience in creating a digital tool through which citizens can report issues and direct them to the relevant departments.

The process has also involved working with the Municipality of Prishtina as we prepare for the pilot phase of the project, which is a different scope of work from Sbunker's focus on media and public debate.

Our role as a capacity hub has also given us an opportunity to work more closely with individual grantees and other civil society organizations, learn about their projects in digital democracy, and the challenges in their communities.

Taken together, these activities have expanded Sbunker’s experience from media, analysis and public debate, to developing digital tools and working more closely with civil society organizations and public institutions.

GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

HD: One of the most valuable experiences has been developing something that is intended to have a direct use in people’s everyday lives. With Kosovo.report, we are taking a different approach by developing a platform that citizens can use in their communities and communicate with relevant institutions.

Building the platform has also given us a better sense of what it takes to turn an idea for civic participation into something that works in practice.

The capacity hub and fellowship have added to this experience by allowing us to work with people approaching digital democracy and civic engagement from different projects and contexts.

GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

HD: For us, Kosovo.report is a starting point for what we want to do in the digital democracy area. The current focus is on Prishtina, but we want to take the platform beyond the pilot and explore opportunities to connect with other municipalities and public institutions across Kosovo.

The first phase is helping us see what works, what needs to be improved, and how the platform can better respond to the needs of local communities.

The project has also strengthened Sbunker’s capacity to develop digital approaches to civic participation. We want to build on that experience in our future work by looking more closely at the needs of the communities we work with and explore where digital tools can help address them.

We also want to continue the relationships developed through this project, both with civil society organizations and collaborators, and see where they can lead beyond the project.

Written by Nurbek Bekmurzaev

articles.title: NASA’s Eyes software: October release notes
articles.excerpt: On October 28, 2026, a new version of Eyes on Exoplanets was released. This release added the new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, which is expected to find thousands of new exoplanets.
articles.content:
On October 28, 2026, a new version of Eyes on Exoplanets was released. This release added the new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, which is expected to find thousands of new exoplanets.

When accessing Eyes on Exoplanets from your mobile phone, you can use the augmented reality feature to place the spacecraft in your own living room or kitchen. The menu option will automatically appear for any of the six spacecraft featured in the app, inviting the user to “View in your space”. Just point the mobile device to a flat surface and the spacecraft will appear on the surface. You can size it up and down by pinching to zoom, and also rotate it by using two fingers to twist. Once you have the spacecraft in position, there is an option to take a picture, which you can then share.

Other improvements in this release include adding the James Webb Space Telescope to the observatory list. You can sort all of the exoplanets as filtered by the observatory that discovered them by selecting Browse Destinations –> Observatory, and then find the observatory you are interested in. James Webb has already directly imaged exoplanets and discovered several.

All pulsars with exoplanets are now available for viewing as well, in addition to numerous bug fixes and upgrades.

articles.author: Sumer Loggins
articles.title: Happy 65 Years: NASA’s Johnson Space Center Then and Now
articles.excerpt: Sixty-five years ago, a bold vision took root in Houston: a NASA center dedicated to human spaceflight. Since its founding, NASA’s Johnson Space Center has helped lead the nation’s human spaceflight program, supporting missions from Project Mercury through Artemis.
articles.content:
Sixty-five years ago, a bold vision took root in Houston: a NASA center dedicated to human spaceflight. Since its founding, NASA’s Johnson Space Center has helped lead the nation’s human spaceflight program, supporting missions from Project Mercury through Artemis.

Today, Johnson serves as NASA’s Center of Excellence for Human Spaceflight, and its workforce is helping to usher in a Golden Age of innovation and discovery. Johnson is home to America’s astronaut corps, the Mission Control Center, and the teams behind some of humanity’s greatest achievements in space. As NASA’s human spaceflight programs evolve, Johnson remains at the forefront of these efforts.

Houston is home to NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program, comprising International Space Station operations and commercial partnerships and destinations in low Earth orbit. For missions beyond low Earth orbit, Johnson houses the Moon Base Program⁠ and Orion Program⁠, while NASA’s Human Health and Performance Directorate⁠ and Human Research Program⁠ work to protect crew health and performance as missions extend farther from Earth.

On May 25, 1961, the center’s story began when President John F. Kennedy gave a speech before a joint session of Congress, committing the nation to achieve the goal of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to Earth before the end of the decade.

NASA’s Space Task Group, in charge of America’s human spaceflight program, was already working on Project Mercury to put astronauts into Earth orbit, but with the additional task of a human lunar landing, it soon outgrew its facilities at NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia. The agency decided it needed a dedicated field center for human spaceflight and on Sept. 19, 1961, after evaluating multiple sites around the country, NASA announced that the new Manned Spacecraft Center would be built near Houston, Texas. The agency established the center on Nov. 1, 1961, and construction began in 1962. In 1973, it officially became NASA’s Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center in honor of President Johnson for his ardent support of America’s space program from its foundation.

Manned Spacecraft Center to Johnson Space Center

The Manned Spacecraft Center officially opened on Nov. 1, 1961, and while construction continued on the Clear Lake site, employees worked in 13 leased buildings in southeast Houston. The design phase took six months and construction of the first buildings took 18 months, with the first employees moving onto the new site in late 1963.

Over the decades, the number of buildings grew, and continues to grow, to meet the demands of new spaceflight programs.

Project Management Building

Construction of the nine-story Project Management Building began on Dec. 5, 1962, and concluded on March 15, 1964. Robert Gilruth, the center’s first director, moved into his office on March 5, 1964, on the top floor of the edifice then known as Building 2. The building swapped numbers with the Public Affairs Building, originally known as Building 1, on June 30, 1974.

Neutral buoyancy spacewalk training

The use of neutral buoyancy for spacewalk training began with the Gemini XII mission in 1966. In 1967, workers installed an above-ground circular pool called the Water Immersion Facility for astronaut training that supported Apollo and pre-Shuttle spacewalk training.. To accommodate the larger size of the space shuttle payload bay, spacewalk training moved to the Weightless Environment Training Facility iin 1980. Astronauts used it for nearly all shuttle spacewalk training until 1997, when the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in the Sonny Carter Training Center entered operations for both shuttle and space station training, as well as testing future space suits and lunar surface activities. 

Lunar Receiving Laboratory (Building 37)

To prevent any back contamination from any possible lunar microorganisms, NASA designed the Lunar Receiving Laboratory in Building 37. Construction began in August 1966, with the first employees moving into their offices in June 1967. The astronauts from Apollo 11, 12, and 14 completed their three-week postflight quarantine in the lab, and scientists in the various laboratories studied the lunar samples all the Apollo missions returned.

Following the Apollo program, Life Sciences division and laboratories moved into the building until they relocated in 2017. Following demolition of Building 37, the Lunar Receiving Park, dedicated in 2026, honors the history of the laboratory.

Spacecraft mockup training facilities (Building 9)

Construction of Building 9 began in December 1965 and finished in March 1967. The building initially housed the Technical Services Facility. In April 1969, workers converted a portion of the building to include a mock lunar surface scene, complete with a mockup of a Lunar Module, used by Apollo 11 astronauts. To support the space shuttle program, workers completed an addition that housed the Mockup and Integration Laboratory in September 1974. Astronauts for all 135 shuttle missions used the mockups for training. An extension on the northwest side of thebuilding begun in 1986 and completed in 1988. It received mockups of Space Station Freedom and later of the International Space Station, and the building was renamed the Space Vehicle Mockup Facility. Today, the facility also houses training mockups of NASA’s Orion spacecraft, commercial mockups, and the Active Response Gravity Offload System, known as ARGOS. 

Mission Simulation and Training Facility (Building 5)

Construction of Building 5, the Mission Simulation and Training Facility completed inApril 1965 and began supporting missions beginning with Gemini IV in June 1965. The building originally contained the Gemini spacecraft simulator and a Gemini translation and docking simulator. Apollo program simulators, including a command module and lunar module simulator, began arriving in December 1965. From 1967 and 1978, astronauts used the Water Immersion Facility for spacewalk training. In the early 1970s, the building also housed full-scale, high-fidelity trainers and simulators of Skylab’s components, which all nine Skylab astronauts used for mission training. In the late 1970s, the facility underwent major renovations to support the space shuttle program, with the addition of fixed base and motion base simulators. The Space Station Training Facility addition, completed in 1991, supported first Space Station Freedom and now International Space Station crew training, and also contains Orion and Starliner simulators.  

Mission Control Center

Construction of Building 30 housing the Mission Control Center began in June 1963 and finished in November 1964, with technicians installing the real-time computer in April 1964 and the first employees moving in two months later. The center initially housed two mission operations control rooms to support Gemini and Apollo missions and simulations. By January 1965, the center monitored the uncrewed Gemini 2 mission and the crewed Gemini 3 mission in a flight following mode.  

In June 1965, Houston had full control of Gemini IV and has controlled each of NASA’s human space flight missions ever since. The control center received a major upgrade to its computer systems in the mid-1970s to support upcoming space shuttle flights. On April 4, 2011, the building was renamed the Christopher C. Kraft, Jr. Mission Control Center, in honor of the man who created the concepts still in use today in human spaceflight control. The control center continues to support the space station around the clock as well as Artemis missions taking humans back to the Moon.

articles.author: Meagan Chappell
articles.title: TB 26-09 Measured Hammer-Tap Inputs
articles.excerpt: For more information, contact Joel W. Sills, Langley Research Center, joel.w.sills@nasa.gov.
articles.content:
For more information, contact Joel W. Sills, Langley Research Center, joel.w.sills@nasa.gov.

Download the PDF version

An instrumented hammer test does not require an idealized single half-sine waveform. When the complete force and response are measured accurately, crest ripples and separated contacts remain known inputs. Force shape changes excitation, but does not inherently invalidate the record. Adequacy depends on measurement accuracy, bandwidth, signal-to-noise ratio, and coverage of the test objective.

Background: What the Hammer Actually Measures
Hammer tests support modal analysis [2–4] and can precede pyroshock testing [6]. Figure 1 compares a half-sine, maintained-contact rippling, and separated contacts. During a zero-force interval, the structure continues to vibrate; re-contact acts on that vibration.

If an exact model and test article receive the same force and initial conditions, uniqueness gives identical responses for each bounded measured history. An approximate model can show different errors as inputs excite different frequencies, amplitudes, or nonlinear states. See [1] for the exact-model derivation.

Analysis: A Half-Sine Is Broadband, but Not Flat
Figure 2 shows that a finite half-sine is broadband but contains spectral zeros at f/fo = 3, 5, 7, …, with fo = 1/(2T) for pulse duration T. Its appearance alone cannot establish adequate excitation.

Analysis: Spectral Content Is Determined by the Measured Force History
Figure 3 normalizes each spectrum to its own DC value. Crest rippling adds content and can fill half-sine notches. Timing between separated contacts creates deterministic interference. For adequacy, inspect the unnormalized measured spectrum and response signal-to-noise ratio.

Recommended Practice: Evaluate Test Adequacy Against the Intended Objective
• Measure the complete applied force with adequate bandwidth, calibration, dynamic range, and time synchronization.
 • Verify that the response measurements have adequate bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio and are not clipped or saturated.
 • Confirm that the excitation covers the frequency, amplitude, and nonlinear-response ranges required by the intended test objective.
• Reject or repeat a test only for an identified measurement, excitation, or coverage deficiency.

Conclusion
Half-sine appearance neither establishes validity nor guarantees adequacy. Judge each hammer test by its purpose and by accurate, complete force and response measurements over the required range.

References
1. A. Majed, J. Sills, E. Henkel, V. Babuska, S. Yunis, D. Hamilton, J. Akers, and T. Kinney, Validity and Predictability of Measured Hammer Tap Inputs: Linear and Nonlinear Structural Systems, September 2026.
2. D. J. Ewins, Modal Testing: Theory, Practice and Application, 2nd ed., 2000.
3. ISO 7626-5:2019, Mechanical Vibration and Shock—Experimental Determination of Mechanical Mobility—Part 5
4. K. G. McConnell and P. S. Varoto, Vibration Testing: Theory and Practice, 2nd ed., 2008.
5. A. H. Nayfeh and D. T. Mook, Nonlinear Oscillations, 1979. 6. NASA-STD-7003, Pyroshock Test Criteria, 1999

articles.author: Leda Zimmerman | MIT Energy Initiative
articles.title: Powering up for a pivotal moment
articles.excerpt: From a nuclear revival to qubits, the MIT Energy Initiative’s annual research conference tracked deployment of today’s technologies to discovery of tomorrow’s breakthroughs.
articles.content:
Leda Zimmerman | MIT Energy Initiative · MIT News · MIT News republication policy

From a nuclear revival to qubits, the MIT Energy Initiative’s annual research conference tracked deployment of today’s technologies to discovery of tomorrow’s breakthroughs.

Utilizing waste carbon at scale, assessing public trust in artificial intelligence and data centers, and building a quantum toolkit for critical applications were among the topics energy experts explored at the MIT Energy Initiative (MITEI)’s annual research conference on Sept. 22-23.

The complexity of the energy transition demands “a truly interdisciplinary and international approach,” said Paula Hammond, Institute Professor and dean of the MIT School of Engineering, kicking off the conference, which was themed “Transitioning energy at a pivotal moment.” 

More than 200 people attended Energizing@MIT: MITEI’s Annual Research Conference in person and online, including faculty, scientists, and researchers; representatives of global energy firms; nonprofit organizations; and academic institutions.

With the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence and data centers, the challenge of the energy transition grows ever greater, requiring “researchers who can pursue fundamental questions about materials, chemistry, and energy systems … engineers who can design new technologies and determine how they might function at scale … and experts in economics, policy, human behavior, and sociology who can help us understand how those technologies will interact with communities and with the world around us,” said Hammond. 

From keynote speakers to panelists, seed grant innovators to startup entrepreneurs, the conference featured exemplars in all these categories.

Deploying today’s technologies

Eric Toone, chief technical officer and managing partner at Breakthrough Energy, set the tone for day one with a keynote address that was clear-eyed in his assessment. “If energy is prosperity,” he told the audience, “at least today, prosperity is emissions.” Yet, Toone was optimistic when he heralded examples of Breakthrough Energy-funded ventures, from iron-air batteries to vacuum-insulated glass windows, which can reduce the carbon costs of energy. 

“We can absolutely develop new technologies that provide the exact same service, but at zero carbon,” he said.

The conference made Toone’s claim tangible as it spanned the full arc of decarbonization — from deploying what we know today to uncovering what may be possible tomorrow. 

There are “projects that are actually being developed, companies that are putting steel in the ground now, electrons onto the grid to deliver capacity now, or in the very, very near term,” said John Parsons, deputy director for research at the MIT Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research. Parsons moderated a panel on the revival of nuclear fission power. 

Highlights included Crane Clean Energy Center’s restoration of the Three Mile Island Unit 1 nuclear plant, set to restart in mid-2027; work by Électricité de France (EDF) to extend and modernize France’s 57-reactor nuclear fleet, adapting plants to climate impacts; and GE Vernova’s development of mature light-water reactor technology, with a new plant under construction in Ontario.

Carbon utilization offers another path to mitigating carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions. “The land and ocean are passively taking up almost 50 percent of anthropogenic CO2 emissions,” said Carolyn Ruppel, MITEI’s deputy director for science and technology, who moderated the panel. “The idea is to find uses for some of the rest of it.” The session showcased research exploring a host of technologies for making products with captured CO2.

Nicola Ferralis, a research scientist in the MIT Department of Materials Science and Engineering (DMSE), highlighted the importance of large-scale uses for carbon waste, such as structural carbon for vehicles and buildings. “We need to find applications that are actually able to match the supply by mass,” he said. 

Admir Masic, an associate professor in the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering and DMSE, described self-heating concrete panels used in real-world conditions in Sapporo, Japan, as well as new concrete materials that can store energy.

“The pace of the transition to a renewable-energy economy will strongly rely on the availability of scalable, bulk energy-storage solutions,” said Masic.

Kripa K. Varanasi, a professor in the MIT Department of Mechanical Engineering, is working on ways to make technologies such as emissions-plume capture at power plants economically viable. 

In a panel devoted to startups with links to MITEI or MITEI member companies, speakers described moving novel energy technologies from research to commercialization: Alfredo Rivela of Adaion has developed an AI tool for electrical utilities that optimizes their use of the grid; Eddie Obropta of Raptor Maps trains drones to inspect solar farms; Michele Guarnieri’s HiBot has created a robot that detects issues in power lines; and Michael Wang of Lithios is conducting field pilots that use electrochemistry to separate lithium from low-grade brines.

Successful ventures, the speakers agreed, begin with a clear customer problem that can be validated by industry users and that offers a path to scaled deployment. For industry users, “innovation is not a corporate virtue,” said Steve Hellman, managing partner at Alliance Partners. “It’s an existential requirement.”

Early-stage research and basic science

The conference also offered a bounty of promising early research on technologies and approaches for cutting carbon emissions. A panel on MITEI’s Seed Innovation Fund Program projects introduced MIT scientists who are separating and recycling rare earth elements; designing algorithms to decide which power plants should run to meet electricity demand; and modeling the impacts on human and natural systems of development and decarbonization.

A poster session revealed the next generation of energy researchers in such fields as chemistry, architecture, aeronautics and astronautics, and computer science. Graduate students are developing a wide array of technologies for carbon mitigation and new energy systems, such as a steam electrolysis process for hydrogen production; models of end-to-end decarbonization in buildings; and designs for hydrogen- and methane-fueled aircraft.

The conference highlighted the importance of fundamental science in feeding the pipeline of new energy technologies. Wednesday’s keynote speaker, Danna Freedman, the F. G. Keyes Professor of Chemistry at MIT and inaugural director of Quantum@MIT, traced scientists’ evolving capacity to harness quantum computing as a tool for solving a range of problems, including those in energy.

“What we want to do at Q-MIT is solve the hard problem, and the hard problem isn’t developing these ridiculously intricate and beautiful quantum tools,” said Freedman. “It is connecting the quantum tools with the applications that will change the world.”

A companion panel explored one such application: quantum sensing, which leverages fundamental physics to capture a nanoscale view of materials and their properties. For instance, Lukasz Zielinski, scientific advisor to the Integrated Sensing and Measurement Program at SLB, uses a lidar camera with single-photon detectors to identify methane plumes. Moderator Paola Cappellaro, the Ford Professor of Engineering in the MIT Department of Nuclear Science and Engineering, described her work using diamond-based sensors for detecting tiny magnetic fields from battery current, potentially helping measure battery conditions without disturbing the battery electrically. Such quantum sensors, Cappellaro said, can be “practical and impactful.” 

Data centers and public trust

One critical challenge facing energy researchers and industry emerged in sessions throughout the two days: the explosive growth of AI and the energy-hungry data centers that fuel this technology. As Deepjyoti Deka, a MITEI principal research scientist, put it, “the big test for AI right now is whether AI can reduce energy usage, improve efficiency, as well as bring in innovation faster than the rate at which it is going to consume electricity to get trained and deployed.” 

“New ‘hyperscale’ facilities built for artificial intelligence can use more power than entire cities,” said Steve Clemmer, director of energy research in the Climate and Energy Program at the Union of Concerned Scientists, sharing a recent analysis of data center proliferation. With new facilities being 10 to even 10,000 times larger than data centers built just a decade ago, he said, wholesale electricity costs will rise, and “increased reliance on fossil fuels will result in tens of billions of dollars in health damages, and trillions in climate damages.” He noted that decision-makers can mitigate these harmful impacts through clean energy development, strong ratepayer protections, and other safeguards.

Given mounting opposition to data centers, Kathryn Kline Tyndall, associate director of energy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, recommended that industry proponents provide early, accessible information about power, water, quality-of-life, land-use, environmental, and economic impacts, tailored to each community in which they hope to set up shop.

Larry Susskind, the Ford Professor of Urban and Environmental Planning in the MIT Department of Urban Studies and Planning, recommended that developers go further, and demonstrate credible benefits to communities. To achieve this, Susskind suggests a facilitated negotiation process between developers and local groups whose object is a community benefits agreement — a deal that might involve altering the data center design, and providing workforce development, infrastructure investment, and clean energy partnerships.

Ultimately, developers must accept that they can’t rush community acceptance; they have to earn it by giving residents a meaningful role in shaping projects and sharing their benefits. 

“You’re going to have to proceed at the speed of trust,” said Susskind.

Preparations continue for the second in the final series of spacewalks to upgrade the International Space Station’s power generation system on Thursday. Meanwhile, the Expedition 75 crew focused its research efforts on life science at the beginning of the week.

Flight engineers Joshua Kutryk of CSA (Canadian Space Agency) and Anil Menon of NASA will install the eighth and final roll-out solar array during a spacewalk planned to start at 8:30 a.m. EST on Thursday. The duo will work on the orbital outpost’s starboard truss structure opposite from the port truss structure where they installed a roll-out solar array on Oct. 29.

Upon completion of the installation job, which is expected to take about seven hours, the station’s power generating capacity will increase about 30 percent from 160 kilowatts to about 215 kilowatts. NASA+ begins its live spacewalk coverage at 7 a.m. on Thursday and also will stream on a variety of other platforms.

Kutryk and Menon joined NASA flight engineers Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney on Monday and studied the Canadarm2 robotic arm procedures necessary to support Thursday’s spacewalk. The quartet also called down to mission controllers for a pair of pre-spacewalk conferences. The astronauts first discussed their mission readiness with spacewalk specialists then spoke to robotics engineers afterward about any Canadarm2 concerns.

Microgravity research was still on Monday’s schedule for the astronauts as they helped researchers advance human health on Earth and in space. Kutryk strapped on the Bio-Monitor’s sensor-packed vest and headband at the beginning of his shift and pedaled on the Destiny laboratory module’s exercise cycle. Results may show how an astronaut’s cardiorespiratory system adapts to weightlessness informing crew health measures on future missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond. Delaney nourished growing vascular tissues samples that were printed inside the BioFabrication Facility. Watkins verified the operation of a portable DNA sequencer used to genetically analyze antibiotic-resistant bacteria in microgravity.

Expedition 75’s three cosmonauts stayed focused on their task list of space research and lab maintenance inside the orbiting complex’s Roscosmos segment. Station commander Pyotr Dubrov continued studying how to manufacture high-purity semiconductor crystals in microgravity that are superior to those produced on Earth. Flight engineer Sergey Teteryatnikov attached electrodes to himself for a 24-hour session measuring his heart activity and blood pressure. Flight engineer Anna Kikina worked on ventilation system maintenance then worked on cargo transfers inside the Progress 96 cargo spacecraft.

Learn more about station activities by following the space station blog, @space_station on X, as well as the ISS Facebook and ISS Instagram accounts.

articles.author: Vanessa Thomas
articles.title: NASA’s Twin ESCAPADE Spacecraft to Slingshot Past Earth on Way to Mars
articles.excerpt: In a few days, NASA’s ESCAPADE (Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers) will perform a maneuver that no agency spacecraft has flown before — and do it twice. Each of the two ESCAPADE spacecraft will execute a “powered” flyby of Earth, combining Earth’s gravity with an engine burn, to slingshot itself toward Mars.
articles.content:
In a few days, NASA’s ESCAPADE (Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers) will perform a maneuver that no agency spacecraft has flown before — and do it twice. Each of the two ESCAPADE spacecraft will execute a “powered” flyby of Earth, combining Earth’s gravity with an engine burn, to slingshot itself toward Mars.

The first spacecraft will conduct its flyby and engine burn around 5 a.m. EST on Saturday, Nov. 7, and the second will do so two days later, around 6 a.m. EST on Monday, Nov. 9. As each spacecraft flies close to Earth, our planet’s gravity will speed it up and redirect it toward Mars. At the spacecraft’s closest approach to Earth, it also will perform a “trans-Mars injection burn,” firing its engine for about 9 minutes to give itself an extra boost toward the Red Planet.

The trans-Mars injection burn will increase each spacecraft’s speed by more than 1,000 miles per hour, or from about 6.3 miles per second to about 6.7 miles per second (from about Mach 30 to Mach 31). At that final speed, the spacecraft could fly from Washington, D.C., to San Francisco in less than 7 minutes.

After completing their successful powered flybys, the two spacecraft will then have a 10-month cruise to Mars, arriving at the Red Planet on Sept. 7 and Sept. 9, 2027, respectively.

At Mars, ESCAPADE will become the first multi-spacecraft mission to fly in formation around the planet. The ESCAPADE mission will study how a million-mile-per-hour stream of material flowing from the Sun, known as the solar wind, interacts with the Martian environment and how that drives atmospheric loss at Mars.

Some spacecraft have used Earth flybys to direct themselves to other destinations in the solar system, but no Mars-bound spacecraft has successfully executed a powered flyby, also known as an Oberth maneuver. Previous missions that reached Mars launched from Earth at a time when the two planets were aligned in space — which only happens every 26 months — to shorten the trip and use the least amount of fuel. However, ESCAPADE launched in November 2025, when Earth and Mars were on opposite sides of the Sun. Instead of heading directly to Mars, ESCAPADE pioneered a new route. The two spacecraft flew in a kidney-bean-shaped loop around a place in space called the Earth-Sun Lagrange point 2 and then headed back toward Earth so they could use Earth’s gravity to propel themselves toward the Red Planet once the planets returned to alignment, which is now.

This unique route already has allowed ESCAPADE to collect some “bonus” science as the spacecraft flew through a distant region of Earth’s magnetotail, a part of Earth’s magnetic environment that gets stretched out away from Earth by the solar wind. No spacecraft had directly explored that part of Earth’s magnetotail before. Mission scientists report that ESCAPADE observed some interesting activity and structure in the magnetotail and are planning to share those findings soon.

As the two ESCAPADE spacecraft perform their Earth flybys on Nov. 7 and 9, some observers on the ground might be able to spot them, though the spacecraft will be faint and a telescope will most likely be needed to find them as dim points moving against the stars. At their closest approach to Earth, the spacecraft, which are each about the size of a standard refrigerator, will be between 600 and 1,100 miles above the planet’s surface, which is higher than most Earth-orbiting satellites.

Each spacecraft will fire its engine as it flies over southern Australia and should be visible with telescopes from there. The first spacecraft’s engine burn will begin at 4:51 a.m. EST (or 8:51 p.m. Australia Eastern Daylight Time, AEDT) on Nov. 7. The second spacecraft’s burn will begin at 5:51 a.m. EST (or 9:51 p.m. AEDT) on Nov. 9.

In the hours leading up to the flybys, each ESCAPADE spacecraft should be visible in the skies over the western U.S. until about an hour before its engine burn, at which point the spacecraft will slip below the horizon. This means the first spacecraft will likely be brightest for the western U.S. between midnight and 1 a.m. PST in the early morning of Nov. 7, and the second one will be brightest between 1 and 2 a.m. PST on Nov. 9.

Each spacecraft will appear to move through the sky relatively slowly and take several hours to cross from east to west overhead.

If you would like to try to spot the ESCAPADE spacecraft with a telescope, you can use the NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory’s Horizons System to get coordinates for the two spacecraft at various times for your viewing location.

Several days after ESCAPADE’s trans-Mars injection burns, the mission team will know how well the spacecraft are aimed for Mars. The team will use multiple trajectory correction maneuvers to adjust the path of the two spacecraft during their journey to Mars, ensuring they are on a precise course to rendezvous with the Red Planet in September next year.

by Vanessa Thomas
NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, Md.

articles.title: What’s Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips from NASA
articles.excerpt: Catch Taurid and Leonid meteors, spot Mars near Jupiter, celebrate Voyager 1’s light-day milestone, and watch November’s supermoon.
articles.content:
Meteor Showers, a Spacecraft Milestone, and a Supermoon

Catch Taurid and Leonid meteors, spot Mars near Jupiter, celebrate Voyager 1’s light-day milestone, and watch November’s supermoon.

Skywatching Highlights

  • Around Nov. 5: Southern Taurids peak; occasional bright fireballs
  • Around Nov. 12: Northern Taurids peak; around five meteors per hour under ideal conditions
  • Nov. 15-16: Mars and Jupiter appear 1.2 degrees apart before sunrise
  • Nov. 17: Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day activation
  • Nov. 17-18: Leonids before dawn after moonset; up to around 15 meteors per hour under ideal conditions
  • Nov. 24: Full supermoon; first in a series of three consecutive supermoons

Transcript

A month of meteor showers … a close pairing of Mars and Jupiter … and a supermoon!

That’s What’s Up for November.

November offers a buffet of opportunities to see a meteor streak across the sky!

The Southern Taurids peak around November 5th, followed by the Northern Taurids around November 12th.

Those names refer to the two areas in the constellation Taurus, where the meteors appear to originate.

Each Taurid shower produces only a handful of meteors per hour—around five, under ideal conditions—but an occasional bright fireball can make the wait worthwhile.

Next up are the Leonids. For the best viewing times, try the early morning hours of November 17th and 18th, after the Moon sets. Under ideal conditions, the shower could produce around 15 meteors per hour, though most viewers will see fewer.

To level up your viewing experience, you will want to find a dark location, give your eyes about half an hour to adjust, and take in as much sky as you can.

Around mid-month, there’s another reason to head outside early. On the mornings of November 15th and 16th, look southeast before sunrise to see Mars and Jupiter close together.

They’ll appear about 1.2 degrees apart—a little more than the width of two full Moons side by side. Jupiter is the brighter point of light, with reddish Mars nearby.

Both planets are easy to see with the unaided eye. They’re still far apart in space, but from Earth, they appear almost side by side.

Watch over several mornings to see them draw closer together – and then go their separate ways.

This month, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft will reach a historic milestone, becoming the first human-made object to travel one light-day from Earth.

That means a signal traveling at the speed of light takes 24 hours to reach the spacecraft – and another 24 hours for us to hear back from it!

If you want to imagine where Voyager 1 is currently traveling, look in the direction of the constellation Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer.

And on November 17th, join us in celebrating this milestone by participating in our Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day activation. Learn more at nasa.gov/voyager.

On November 24th, the evening sky will be lit by a supermoon.

Because the Moon’s orbit is slightly oval, its distance from Earth changes. When it’s closer, the full Moon appears larger and brighter than average – though the difference can be subtle.

This kicks off a series of three consecutive supermoons in November, December, and January.

Look east around sunset to watch it rise. It may look even bigger near the horizon, but that’s the Moon illusion —a common effect with any full Moon.

Here are the phases of the Moon for November:

articles.author: Civic Media Observatory
articles.title: The Brazilian left’s quest to ‘tame’ Meta: A narrative of denouncement and resistance
articles.excerpt: Internet rights advocates and Lula da Silva campaigners challenge Meta’s alleged shadow banning
articles.content:
This story by Civic Media Observatory originally appeared on Global Voices. Text licensed under CC BY 3.0. Reformatted for reading; third-party media omitted.

Internet rights advocates and Lula da Silva campaigners challenge Meta’s alleged shadow banning

This story is part of Undertones, Global Voices’ Civic Media Observatory’s newsletter and column. Subscribe to Undertones here. It is also part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Over the years, Meta’s content moderation policies and governance practices have faced intense scrutiny and legal challenges over alleged political bias and a lack of transparency.

Since 2018, the Arab Center for Social Media Advancement (7amleh), a human rights organization advocating for Palestinian digital rights, has documented how Facebook’s (now Meta) moderation practices disproportionately affect Palestinian content. In 2020, 7amleh launched a campaign challenging Facebook’s proposed hate speech policy, which considered “Zionist” a potential proxy for “Jew” or “Jewish.” More recently, in 2024, the organization collected 20 first-hand testimonies from Palestinian influencers, journalists, and media outlets documenting their experiences of Meta’s discriminatory content moderation practices. In 2023, Human Rights Watch also reported “systemic online censorship” against voices in support of Palestine and Palestinian human rights,

In 2022, Tom Vandendriessche, a Belgian politician and Member of the European Parliament (MEP) representing the far-right Vlaams Belang (Flemish Interest) party, partially prevailed in a legal case against Meta concerning a shadow ban imposed on his account in 2021 after the company removed several posts alleging a breach of its Terms of Service (ToS) and Facebook Community Guidelines (FCG). A Belgian court ordered the company to compensate the politician for financial and reputational damages, finding that its actions had significantly restricted his ability to engage in political discourse online and that Meta had failed to provide adequate transparency or effective avenues for redress.

In 2026, Meta has faced significant criticism in Brazil and internationally from internet rights watchdogs over political bias, algorithmic interference, and the selective suppression of content perceived as favoring far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro during the October 2026 Brazilian presidential election.

Narrative: Meta, take your hands off our election!

Using the slogan Meta não se meta (roughly, “Meta, stay out of it”), which plays on the Portuguese word meta, derived from the verb meter (“to get involved” or “to interfere”), internet rights defenders and current President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s followers and allies sought not only to expose alleged Meta’s shadow-banning practices during Brazil’s 2026 presidential election but also to mobilize Brazilians to demand a fairer digital space collectively. 

Sub-narrative: We demand digital sovereignty, and we will hold Meta accountable

In October 2026, during the Brazilian presidential runoff election campaign, a coalition of Brazilian civil society organizations, social movements, and digital rights advocacy groups, including CTRL+Z, Código Não Binário, ARTIGO 19 (Article 19 Brasil), Sleeping Giants Brasil, and others, launched the webpage naosemeta.com.br as part of their initiative to denounce electoral interference and algorithmic bias. The site offered three ways for people to hold Meta accountable online: email Meta; message Meta’s General Director in Brazil on LinkedIn; and comment on Meta Ceo Mark Zuckerberg’s latest Instagram post. It also shared a space for those wishing to join and sign a petition to the Superior Electoral Court and an extrajudicial notification, a formal written communication sent on October 19 to put Meta on notice and demand that it recognize the technical flaws in its advertising, moderation, and artificial intelligence (AI) systems, and the distribution and availability of user-generated content and campaign materials in Brazil — which these organizations claim disadvantaged, in particular, candidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

The online strategy to hold Meta accountable was accompanied by a protest in front of Meta’s offices on October 19, where participants called for respect for Brazil’s digital sovereignty, with the Homeless Workers Movement’s Technology Center among the loudest voices.

For those reclaiming digital sovereignty, the company’s actions stem from the relationship between U.S. President Donald Trump and Brazil’s ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, father of Flávio Bolsonaro, and the influence the current U.S. administration has over big-tech owners — they consider Meta to be facilitating foreign interference.

Sub-narrative: Together, we can “tame” the algorithm

An extra layer supported the narrative “Meta, take your hands off our election!” After the first round of the election gave candidate Flávio Bolsonaro a small lead in early October, left-wing Congressman André Janones relaunched his WhatsApp channel, “Lula’s Army,” an initiative to mobilize voters online and offline and give visibility to Lula da Silva’s messaging and proposals, and that quickly gained millions of followers.

In addition to reclaiming Brazilian symbols from the far-right, including inviting followers to wear the country’s yellow soccer team T-shirt, the WhatsApp channel coordinated social media interactions to boost Lula da Silva’s visibility. By giving his “troops” instructions on when and how to engage with the content Lula da Silva’s campaign produced, Janones positioned an implicit narrative that argued it was possible to “tame” the algorithm, regain ownership of the Brazilian digital media ecosystem, and ultimately win the election, recapturing the campaign spirits.

After Lula da Silva’s unprecedented second-round comeback on October 25, this narrative evolved to “dobramos a Meta,” which translates to “we doubled Meta,” hinting at the “dobrar a meta” (doubled the target) popular meme that originated from a statement made by former Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff in July 2015, during a speech on the National Program for Access to Technical Education and Employment (PRONATEC)— all to say “we were able to overcome Meta’s content moderation policies and governance.”

The context surrounding the narrative

Brazil ranks as the world’s second-largest country by WhatsApp users (148 million) and the third-largest addressable Instagram audience (147 million). The country is considered a pioneer in internet governance and digital regulation, with a strong tradition of open, multistakeholder approaches to protecting digital rights, especially thanks to the country's foundational internet law, Federal Law No. 12.965/2014, known as the Marco Civil da Internet.

For more than 10 years, Brazil’s Marco Civil da Internet protected digital platforms from civil liability for third-party content, except when they failed to comply with a specific court order requiring its removal, safeguarding freedom of expression while preventing platforms from being inundated with takedown requests. This changed in June 2025, when the country’s Supreme Court, recognizing shifts in digital media ecosystems, ruled that Federal Law No. 12.965/2014 was partially unconstitutional because it no longer sufficiently protected fundamental rights and democracy. The ruling made digital platforms liable for third parties’ content in Brazil, a decision experts argue is impossible to fulfill until digital platforms offer real transparency into their content moderation policies and governance practices. 

In October 2026, Sleeping Giant Brasil shared a report on what they consider evidence of Meta’s “algorithmic favoritism” toward the Bolsonaros’ political allies, focusing on the case of Nikolas Ferreira, a right-wing politician affiliated with the Liberal Party (PL) — currently serving as a Member of the Chamber of Deputies, elected for a four-year term in 2022.

On October 14, the Brazilian independent news site Nucleo shared an investigation showing how Meta’s AI favored creating images of Flávio Bolsonaro on WhatsApp. According to the outlet, Meta acknowledged the failure via email and said it would take the necessary measures to prevent it from happening again.

On October 15, Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court (TSE) ruled that Meta must refrain from interfering with the distribution of political and electoral content posted by either Lula da Silva or Flávio Bolsonaro until the conclusion of the election’s second round, stating that failure to comply with the ruling would result in a daily fine of BRL 500,000 (USD 91,942). The decision came after Lula da Silva’s reelection campaign team denounced to the TSE that Meta repeatedly restricted the reach of publications linked to the government candidate and his supporters

On October 16, the newspaper Folha de S.Paulo reported that Meta employees acknowledged in internal communications that restrictions during the country's election hindered the Instagram accounts of Lula da Silva.

Meta acknowledged technical issues on its platforms on October 16, but said they were not the result of political bias. In an official statement, the company said the “ad account for Lula’s campaign was deactivated by mistake for just over an hour, and not for political reasons,” and that several of the reported problems were part of a “global” failure. 

In his celebration speech, Lula da Silva promised to prioritize new regulations that ensure big digital media platforms are held accountable. He stated that during the recent election, he and his allies had to “overcome outside interference coming in through digital platforms,” and argued Brazil “cannot have monstrous companies earning billions, paying no taxes, and trying to steer” the country’s elections.

Social media and disinformation have played a central role in past elections in Brazil, as research shared by Harvard Kennedy School’s Misinformation Review, a scholarly publication, argues that in the 2022 election, “susceptibility to electoral misinformation is affected by factors such as political ideology, trust in the electoral process and democratic institutions, and information consumption, with those who participate in political groups in messaging apps being more likely to believe in electoral misinformation.”

As in 2022 but without the coup plot, the Bolsonaro family alleges electoral fraud. In a first letter shared after fleeing the country amid open investigations linking him to money laundering, Flávio Bolsonaro first declared himself “the elected president,” then deleted it and replaced it with a second version calling himself the rightful “leader” of Brazil. Bolsonaro argues in the text that he had to leave the country to prevent political persecution. 

Although Flávio Bolsonaro insisted he would seek to annul the presidential election, his party later distanced itself from that position in a statement and chose to accept the official results, while still reporting irregularities during the electoral process.

Written by Civic Media Observatory, Samanta Azpurua

articles.title: NASA’s Swift Observatory to Re-Enter Atmosphere
articles.excerpt: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is expected to re-enter Earth’s atmosphere on Wednesday, Nov. 4, almost 22 years after launch. At launch, Swift was a first-of-its-kind multiwavelength observatory designed to study the most powerful explosions in the cosmos using its three telescopes.
articles.content:
NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is expected to re-enter Earth’s atmosphere on Wednesday, Nov. 4, almost 22 years after launch. At launch, Swift was a first-of-its-kind multiwavelength observatory designed to study the most powerful explosions in the cosmos using its three telescopes. 

As of Monday, the U.S. Space Force predicted that the roughly 3,200-pound spacecraft will re-enter the atmosphere at approximately 3:30 a.m. EST, Nov. 4, with an uncertainty of 11 hours. NASA expects most of the spacecraft to burn up as it travels through the atmosphere, but some components are expected to survive re-entry. Re-entry locations of any surviving components can vary from hemisphere to hemisphere and depend on when it re-enters. Due to Swift’s low inclination, re-entry locations of surviving fragments are limited between 20.6 degrees south latitude and 20.6 degrees north latitude. The risk of harm coming to anyone on Earth is unlikely — approximately 1 in 2,100. NASA and Space Force will continue to monitor the re-entry and update predictions. 

NASA’s Swift launched in 2004 to explore the universe’s most powerful explosions, called gamma-ray bursts. It was originally designed for a two-year prime mission. During more than two decades of science operations, Swift served as a multi-tool for exploring the universe, observing a wide range of light, rapidly pointing at short-lived outbursts, and sending alerts to other facilities to help coordinate follow-up observations. Swift has broadened our understanding of a wide variety of cosmic objects and events, from active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes and stars undergoing X-ray flares, to supernova explosions and comets and asteroids in our own solar system. 

Monitor NASA’s Swift blog for continued updates:

articles.title: NASA Invites Media to Northrop Grumman CRS-25 Station Resupply Launch
articles.excerpt: Media accreditation is open for the next launch to deliver NASA science investigations, supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station. A Northrop Grumman Cygnus XL spacecraft will launch in November to the orbital laboratory on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket for NASA.
articles.content:
Media accreditation is open for the next launch to deliver NASA science investigations, supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station. A Northrop Grumman Cygnus XL spacecraft will launch in November to the orbital laboratory on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket for NASA.

The mission is known as NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25, or NASA’s Northrop Grumman CRS-25. Liftoff is targeted for no earlier than 10:49 a.m. EST, Sunday, Nov. 29, from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.

Following launch, astronauts aboard the space station will use the Canadarm2 robotic arm to capture Cygnus and install the spacecraft to the Unity module’s Earth-facing port for cargo unloading. The spacecraft will remain at the space station until May 2027. This is the company’s 25th spacecraft built to deliver supplies to the International Space Station under contract with NASA.

Credentialing to cover prelaunch and launch activities is open to U.S. media. The application deadline for U.S. citizens is 11:59 p.m. EST, Thursday, Nov. 12. All accreditation requests must be submitted online at:

https://media.ksc.nasa.gov

Credentialed media will receive a confirmation email following approval. NASA’s media accreditation policy is available online. For questions about accreditation, or to request special logistical support, email: ksc-media-accreditat@mail.nasa.gov. For other questions, please contact NASA’s Kennedy Space Center newsroom at: 321-867-2468.

In addition to food, supplies, and equipment for the crew, Cygnus will deliver several new experiments, including hardware to manufacture tiny, DNA-inspired particles in space that could improve drug delivery for cancer and osteoarthritis, as well as a study that could guide cancer treatments by predicting whether a patient’s cancer is likely to spread to other parts of the body. Cygnus also will carry human muscle cells and medications to test therapeutics for muscle loss associated with spaceflight and aging on Earth, and a compact radiation sensor designed to improve crew safety on future missions. 

Each resupply mission to the station delivers scientific investigations in the areas of biology and biotechnology, Earth and space science, physical sciences, and technology development and demonstrations. Cargo resupply from U.S. companies ensures a national capability to deliver scientific research to the space station, increasing NASA’s ability to conduct new investigations aboard humanity’s laboratory in space.

For 26 years, people have lived and worked continuously aboard the International Space Station, advancing scientific knowledge and making research breakthroughs that are not possible on Earth. The space station is an important testbed for NASA to understand and overcome the challenges of long-duration spaceflight and to expand commercial opportunities in low Earth orbit. As commercial companies concentrate on providing human space transportation services and destinations as part of a strong low Earth orbit economy, NASA is focusing its resources on deep space missions to the Moon as part of the Artemis and Moon Base programs to build on our foundation for the first astronaut missions to Mars.

Learn more about International Space Station research and operations at:

https://www.nasa.gov/station

articles.author: Jillian C. York
articles.title: Independent Digital Media Is Not a Privilege Governments Can Revoke: The Fight to Save Egypt’s Mada Masr
articles.excerpt: On November 11, Lina Attalah, founder and editor-in-chief of the independent Egyptian news outlet Mada Masr, will face trial for the second time in just two weeks. This time, she faces charges of spreading false news, an accusation that has become one of the Egyptian government's most frequently used tools for prosecuting journalists.
articles.content:
Jillian C. York · Electronic Frontier Foundation · CC BY 4.0

On November 11, Lina Attalah, founder and editor-in-chief of the independent Egyptian news outlet Mada Masr, will face trial for the second time in just two weeks. This time, she faces charges of spreading false news, an accusation that has become one of the Egyptian government's most frequently used tools for prosecuting journalists. 

The trial follows a conviction on October 27, when Attalah was found guilty of managing an unlicensed news website. The Mada Masr team had repeatedly applied for a license, but their attempts went unacknowledged. The proceedings took place in a single hearing, which Mada Masr states included serious violations of her right to a fair trial. She was sentenced to the maximum fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds (approximately 55,000 USD), forcibly removed from the courtroom, and held for seven hours until the fine was paid. The court also ordered Mada Masr's closure and the confiscation of all equipment belonging to the organization. 

The current wave of repression has also targeted Matsada2sh, a fact-checking and open-source intelligence initiative. Its entire six-person newsroom was violently arrested, illegally detained, and interrogated under torture before being charged with terrorism-related offenses and spreading false news. The team remains in pretrial detention. 

According to CPJ, at least 25 other journalists are currently incarcerated in Egypt. 

Governments seeking to control the flow of information increasingly rely on a combination of legal harassment, financial pressure, criminal prosecution, and restrictions on the infrastructure that makes independent publishing possible. Egypt's media licensing regime is a particularly troubling example. Requiring news organizations to obtain government authorization to operate creates an obvious mechanism for restricting who gets to publish and whose voices are allowed to reach the public.  

The charge of spreading false news is similarly dangerous. Governments around the world have increasingly invoked the language of misinformation to justify restrictions on speech, often without meaningful safeguards against political abuse, as we laid out in our recent submission to the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights. Governments should never be the arbiters of which reporting is permissible, particularly when that reporting concerns their own conduct. 

Why Mada Masr matters 

Founded in 2013, Mada Masr has spent more than a decade doing the kind of journalism that authoritarian governments find most threatening: documenting abuses, amplifying marginalized voices, and reporting on issues that powerful institutions would prefer remain hidden. 

Its reporting has given torture survivors and the families of political prisoners a platform. It has opened space for debate about reproductive rights. It has brought frontline reporting from Sudan and Gaza, and stood alongside refugees facing xenophobic attacks and security crackdowns. 

Emerging as a digital-first publication, in a media environment where traditional outlets were increasingly constrained, being purely digital allowed Mada Masr’s founders to build an independent publication outside the structures of legacy media.  

At a time when only 43% of Egyptians had access to the internet, going fully digital meant taking a big risk, but it was one that has been rewarding: Despite being blocked by the Egyptian government since 2017, Mada Masr has continued to reach Egyptian and global audiences, and Attalah has received numerous accolades, including the Knight International Journalism Award, the Ordre des Arts et des Lettres, and a spot in TIME Magazine’s 100 most influential people (2020). 

Mada Masr has also consistently engaged with technology and advocated for a free and independent internet for the global majority. It has covered dozens of hot-button tech stories in recent years, from Egypt’s Cybercrime Bill and Israel’s use of AI weaponry in Gaza, to stories about the “privacy chaos” caused by biometrics to more personal essays about the importance of the internet and tech. In August, they launched an open call for proposals on original critical reporting on artificial intelligence. 

Mada Masr may be thoroughly Egyptian, but it doesn’t belong just to Egypt. Its team has made into a publication that represents the kind of independent, local, grounded journalism that international audiences need, particularly at a time when international reporting on state repression is lacking. They built on-the-ground networks to center local voices in Sudan (publishing in both English and Arabic on the conflict) and Gaza out of a sense of cross-border responsibility and solidarity. 

This is precisely why its potential closure should concern everyone who cares about a free press. The ability to publish independently, investigate powerful institutions, and to share information without government interference is fundamental to the exercise of free expression.  

From solidarity to action 

The international community has repeatedly expressed concern about restrictions on press and internet freedom in Egypt. More than 100 organizations have now joined statements of solidarity with Mada Masr, and with Matsada2sh.  

These expressions of support matter, particularly when journalists are increasingly isolated and under threat—but solidarity must also translate into sustained political and institutional pressure. 

The international governments and institutions that maintain relationships with Egypt—including those in the European Union, the United Kingdom, and the United States—should make clear that the prosecution of journalists and the forced closure of independent media outlets are unacceptable.  

The cases against Lina Attalah, Mada Masr, and Matsada2sh must be dropped. The journalists who remain in detention must be released. And Egypt's licensing regime, with its profound chilling effects on access to information and independent knowledge production, must be brought to an end. 

There is a particular urgency to defending independent media at a moment when governments are finding ever more ways to restrict the circulation of information. Whether through internet shutdowns, platform restrictions, surveillance, or the criminalization of reporting, the result is often the same: fewer opportunities for people to understand what is happening around them, to challenge official narratives, and to hold power accountable. 

We cannot allow the closure of one of Egypt's most important independent newsrooms and the prosecution of its editor-in-chief to become another routine episode in the global erosion of press freedom. Nor should we wait until the last independent journalists have been silenced before recognizing what has been lost. 

To learn more about Lina Attalah in her own reads, you can read our Speaking Freely interview from January 2026.

articles.title: NASA’s Hubble Uncovers Case of Missing Oxygen in Nearby Dwarf Galaxies
articles.excerpt: NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope just revealed a mystery in our cosmic neighborhood. In a paper published Monday in The Astrophysical Journal, researchers using Hubble studied 37 nearby dwarf galaxies — small galaxies containing a few thousand to hundreds of millions of stars — and found that much of the oxygen they expected to see is missing.
articles.content:
NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope just revealed a mystery in our cosmic neighborhood. In a paper published Monday in The Astrophysical Journal, researchers using Hubble studied 37 nearby dwarf galaxies — small galaxies containing a few thousand to hundreds of millions of stars — and found that much of the oxygen they expected to see is missing. 

Simulations predict that significantly more oxygen, a tracer of a wider set of heavy elements, should reside in these galaxies. So where did it go? 

“Oxygen is produced by stars, which are inside of galaxies. We know that the oxygen had to be inside of the galaxies at some point in the past, so the oxygen must have been ejected,” said co-investigator Grace Telford, assistant professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Utah. “And to do that, you need energy from massive stars and supernova explosions to drive material out of the host galaxies and into the space between galaxies.”

Galactic winds unleashed by supernovae are apparently more effective at removing oxygen from low-mass galaxies than current models predict, according to the new study. The findings show that dwarf galaxies can hold onto only a small fraction of the oxygen made by stars. 

In the Galaxies Losing Oxygen via Winds (GLOW) project, funded by NASA and the National Science Foundation, scientists traced the oxygen to understand how it is distributed inside stars, in the gas between stars, and in the space between galaxies. But, of all the elements in the galaxies, why study oxygen?

Oxygen, the most abundant element after hydrogen and helium, is relatively easy to detect and measure, and its production is well understood — making it a reliable indicator of how chemical elements are distributed in a galaxy. 

“So, it’s really for practical reasons that we’ve chosen oxygen,” said Kristen Wingfield McQuinn, GLOW principal investigator and mission head of the Science Operations Center for NASA’s newly launched, panoramic Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, Maryland. She also is an associate professor at Rutgers University in New Brunswick, New Jersey. 

“Oxygen is one of the primary elements formed by stars. Being able to trace how much oxygen gets made, and then how much is distributed inside and outside of galaxies, helps us understand galaxy evolution,” said McQuinn. “It also helps us learn where and how much galaxies are enriching the space between galaxies, called the intergalactic medium.” 

The study used archival optical imaging data from Hubble to resolve stellar populations and determine star-formation histories and compositions. Along with data from NASA’s retired Spitzer Space Telescope as well as the ground-based Very Large Array and Australian Telescope Compact Array, the researchers analyzed 37 nearby dwarf galaxies to trace oxygen atoms produced by stars. 

The team wanted to understand how oxygen is distributed across the stars, gas, and dust in the galaxies. These dwarf galaxies were selected because their masses fall in the range where simulations and theory predict that an increasing amount of their oxygen will be expelled from the galaxies via supernovae explosions. These 37 galaxies also are all close enough for Hubble to resolve their individual stars. That’s not true for the vast majority of known dwarf galaxies, which are too far away for this kind of study.

Although astronomers already suspected that galaxies expel a large fraction of oxygen and other heavy elements, an open question has been where these metals end up. A previous study from 2014 addressed this question for Milky Way-like, star-forming galaxies, finding that these galaxies lost a large fraction of their oxygen, some of which is found in the diffuse haloes of gas surrounding galaxies outside their disks, called the circumgalactic medium.

In the GLOW study, McQuinn and her team extended this research to low-mass galaxies across a wide range of masses and environments. While previous teams have measured oxygen in the circumgalactic medium of dwarf galaxies, it is still unclear if most of the missing oxygen is in this region, or if it has been completely ejected from the galaxy’s surroundings. 

In the future, McQuinn hopes to study even lower-mass galaxies in the nearby universe. She has an approved program to use the Roman Space Telescope to find these faint and tiny systems across a wide swath of sky. Once she’s identified these galaxies, McQuinn hopes to use Hubble and NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope to get deeper observations of their stars. This would allow her to reconstruct the galaxies’ histories to understand how they formed stars across cosmic time. 

Telford’s future work involves using Hubble to zoom in on the individual, massive stars that produce oxygen and eject it from their host galaxies. She’s using some of the nearby GLOW targets to get very detailed observations to characterize how the massive stars are different in these small galaxies.

The Hubble Space Telescope has been operating for over three decades and continues to make ground-breaking discoveries that shape our fundamental understanding of the universe. Hubble is a project of international cooperation between NASA and ESA (European Space Agency). NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, manages the telescope and mission operations. Lockheed Martin Space, based in Denver, also supports mission operations at Goddard. The Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, which is operated by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy, conducts Hubble science operations for NASA.

articles.title: Regina Barzilay and Jim Collins win Pritzker Prize for AI and Science Research Excellence for work in AI-enabled antibiotic discovery
articles.excerpt: The MIT professors collaborated to identify the first AI-discovered antibiotic, a scientific breakthrough that is widely recognized as a milestone in AI-driven drug discovery.
articles.content:
Alex Ouyang | Abdul Latif Jameel Clinic for Machine Learning in Health · MIT News · MIT News republication policy

The MIT professors collaborated to identify the first AI-discovered antibiotic, a scientific breakthrough that is widely recognized as a milestone in AI-driven drug discovery.

Regina Barzilay, MIT’s School of Engineering Distinguished Professor of AI and Health, and James Collins, MIT’s Termeer Professor of Medical Engineering and Science, are the recipients of the 2026 Pritzker Prize for AI in Science Research Excellence. 

The award recognizes their joint work in “pioneering AI-enabled antibiotic discovery, integrating deep learning, bioengineering, and experimental validation to identify novel antibacterial candidates against drug-resistant pathogens.” 

Established in 2024 by the University of Chicago in partnership with Caltech, the Pritzker Prize for AI in Science Research Excellence recognizes contributions that jointly advance AI and the natural sciences or engineering.

Barzilay and Collins, who are faculty co-leads of the Abdul Latif Jameel Clinic for Machine Learning in Health (Jameel Clinic) and affiliates of the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing and the MIT School of Engineering, published their first breakthrough paper together in 2020 with then-MIT postdoc and first author Jonathan Stokes (who worked in the Collins lab from 2017 to 2021) in Cell. The paper described the first artificial intelligence-discovered antibiotic, called halicin, named for the fictional AI system HAL 9000 in Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 film 2001: A Space Odyssey.

A broad-spectrum antibiotic that was originally studied as a potential diabetes drug, halicin was identified by a deep learning model trained on 2,500 molecules. Upon testing, the research team found that halicin was able to kill antibiotic-resistant bacteria (i.e., “superbugs”) such as Clostridium difficile, Acinetobacter baumannii, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. A discovery process that once took years was completed in just a few weeks. Amidst the growing alarm around the global antimicrobial resistance crisis, the results demonstrated that AI could prove to be an effective tool for rapidly identifying new and effective antibiotics.

Following halicin, Barzilay and Collins worked with Stokes (now an assistant professor at McMaster University) to use machine learning to identify abaucin in 2023, a narrow-spectrum antibiotic demonstrating effectiveness against A. baumannii, an antibiotic-resistant bacteria commonly found on hospital doorknobs and in the wounds of U.S. soldiers stationed in Iraq and Afghanistan. Notably, abaucin’s “narrow spectrum” efficacy against a single species of treatment-resistant bacteria is its main advantage, minimizing the likelihood of bacteria developing resistance and harming beneficial bacteria in the gut.

“Historically, antibiotic discovery has depended on laborious, trial-and-error strategies,” says Collins. “This process is slow, costly, and unpredictable, often yielding few viable antibiotic candidates. With generative AI, we're now seeing a shift from AI being used as a tool for discovery to AI being used as a design tool. This shift opens new frontiers in antibiotic discovery that could bring us the next generation of lifesaving drugs.”

In Barzilay’s view, “despite significant progress in molecular modeling, we are still in early stages of drug discovery. With AI, we can only automate parts of the pipeline, rather than totally transforming the discovery process. To make it happen, we need to work really hard to build realistic AI models of human biology.”
